Process engineering

Designing fouling margin you will actually use

Marta Ellison, principal process engineer · 14 January 2026 · 9 minute read

The fouling factor is the most over-specified number on a heat exchanger datasheet, and the one most likely to be copied from the last project without anyone asking what it did there.

Open any tender pack for a preheat train and you will find fouling resistances quoted to three decimal places. Trace them back and they usually come from a table in a standard, applied to a fluid described in two words. The number is not wrong, exactly. It is simply not about this plant.

What it does instead is buy area. A generous fouling allowance makes the exchanger bigger, which makes the clean-condition velocity lower, which makes it foul faster. The margin creates the problem it was specified to absorb. We see the consequence on the service side four or five times a year: a unit that has never once run at its design duty, cleaned twice as often as the model said it would need to be.

Start from the cleaning interval, not the resistance

The question that produces a useful answer is not "what is the fouling factor for this fluid". It is "how often will this plant open this unit, and what duty does it need to hold on the day before it does".

That reframes the design point. Instead of sizing for a fouled steady state that never arrives, you size for the end of the run — the worst hour before the turnaround — and you let the clean-condition performance be whatever it is. In practice this almost always produces a smaller exchanger with higher velocities, which fouls more slowly, which lengthens the run.

Three things worth measuring before you size anything

  1. The actual cleaning history of the incumbent unit. Not the planned interval. The dates the bundle physically came out, for the last five years.
  2. Pressure drop against time, not just duty against time. Duty degrades gently and hides the problem; pressure drop tells you what the deposit is doing to the flow path.
  3. What the deposit is. Ten minutes with a sample and a lab is worth more than a season of correlation. Coke, scale and biofilm behave nothing alike and respond to velocity in opposite directions.

Where the standard tables still help

None of this makes the published resistances useless. They are a reasonable prior when there is genuinely no operating history — a new plant, a new feedstock, a duty nobody in the room has run before. The failure is not using them. The failure is using them when there are five years of maintenance records sitting in the CMMS that nobody pulled.

We halved the fouling allowance, the exchanger came out two shell sizes smaller, and the run length went from eleven months to nineteen. Nobody believed the first number until the second one arrived.

Process engineering manager, Humber refinery

What we do differently on a quotation

When a datasheet arrives with a fouling factor on it, we quote to the datasheet, because that is what was asked for. Then we send a second sheet showing what the unit looks like sized to a cleaning interval, with the assumptions written out so they can be argued with. About a third of the time the second sheet becomes the order.

It is a slower way to sell an exchanger. It is a much faster way to stop selling the same customer a replacement in four years.
